name: Build a simple emergency shelter
blurb: A debris hut is a survival shelter you build with no kit at all: a frame of sticks and a thick pile of leaves that traps your own body heat. Building one badly teaches you why the details matter.
gear: A knife is helpful but not essential
A wooded site with plenty of dead leaf litter
steps: Pick the site: dry, flat, above the valley floor, away from dead branches overhead and not in a water channel.
Build the frame: one sturdy ridgepole from a low fork or stump, long enough to lie under with a little room.
Add ribs at 45 degrees along both sides, closely spaced, then a lattice of small branches to hold debris.
Pile leaf litter over the whole thing to at least an arm’s depth — this is insulation, and thin is useless.
Stuff the inside with a thick bed of dry debris, at least 20 cm compressed, because most heat is lost to the ground.
Make the entrance small and plug it with a debris bundle once inside.
tips: Build it small. A shelter you can barely fit into is a shelter your body can actually heat.
Insulation underneath matters more than the roof. Cold ground steals heat faster than cold air.
A real debris hut takes hours. Start well before dark.
proof: You build one and spend a comfortable hour inside it without a sleeping bag on a cold day.
